notes:
Need to search first.# Research notes on Jeremiah 16

I read Enduring Word (Guzik) in full. Studylight and Biblehub gave me Constable, Gill, Ellicott, Keil & Delitzsch, Matthew Henry, Calvin, Haydock, the Restoration Commentary and others, mostly as excerpts in search results. I also found a few short pieces from catholic.com, Ligonier, TGC and bible.org. My tool limit ran out before I could open the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, the Wesley or Lutheran sites, Orthodox sources, Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word, or Precept Austin's page on chapter 16. So those views are missing below. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Ellicott says this phrase opens a new message that extends to Jeremiah 17:18 and is even more terrible in its threats than anything before it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-1.htm)

**v. 2:**
- Guzik: God's command went against Jeremiah's legitimate wish for marriage and children; to answer God's call he might have to give such things up for a higher calling. He adds that in Jewish culture being single and childless was shameful, so Jeremiah's obedience would draw attention. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- Constable: Bachelors were so rare in Israel that Hebrew has no word for "bachelor," so Jeremiah would have faced much mockery and scorn. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Gill: Jeremiah was told not to marry not because marriage was unlawful (prophets did marry), but because of the coming disasters, which a wife would only make harder to bear.
- Barnes: since marriage was a duty for Jews, forbidding it signalled a calamity so great it overrode ordinary duties.
- Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch both compare Paul's advice "because of the present distress" (1 Cor 7:26). Keil & Delitzsch add that "this place" alternates with "this land," so it means all of Judah, not just Jerusalem. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-2.htm)

**vv. 3–4:**
- Constable: the people of Judah were about to die horrible deaths; exile was close. He also suggests God may have wanted to spare Jeremiah the grief of watching a wife and children die. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Restoration Commentary: the ban may seem harsh but is basically kind, sparing Jeremiah the extra agony of seeing his family destroyed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-16.html)
- Matthew Henry: people with families cannot easily flee, whereas a single man can escape. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_016.cfm)

**v. 5:**
- Guzik: because God had withdrawn His peace, Jeremiah was not to join in formal mourning. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- Constable: Jeremiah's life was meant to remind the people that God had withdrawn from them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Biblehub's study notes say "peace" (shalom) here means God's favour and protection have been removed entirely. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/16.htm)
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah's grief for the whole nation had to replace grief for individual deaths. Those dying just before the judgment arrived could even be counted fortunate, spared the disaster to come. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_016.cfm)

**v. 6:**
- Guzik, citing Thompson: cutting oneself and shaving the head were self-mutilating mourning rites. They seem to have been common in Israel even though the Law forbade them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- Restoration Commentary: so many would die that the survivors could not, and would not want to, hold normal funerals; nobles and commoners alike would go unburied. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-16.html)

**v. 7:** Guzik: no mourning custom would survive the judgment, neither the accepted ones (the funeral meal) nor the pagan ones (cutting). Citing Feinberg, he notes Jeremiah himself would lose the privilege of serving the grieving. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)

**v. 8:**
- Constable: the ban included weddings, and missing weddings and funerals made Jeremiah even more of a social outcast. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Guzik quotes Cundall: in Judah's close-knit community this amounted to a self-imposed excommunication. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)

**v. 9:**
- Ellicott notes the same wording appears in 7:34, 25:10 and 33:11, and the repetition makes it more solemn, not less.
- Gill: "in your days" means it would happen soon, although the people wanted to push such evil days far off. Wedding songs would stop, which would mean ruin for the nation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-9.htm)
- Constable: Jeremiah's withdrawal from village life pictured God's withdrawal from His people. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Biblehub's study notes link this verse to Revelation 18:23, where the same image is used for the fall of Babylon. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/16.htm)

**v. 10:**
- Guzik: God wanted the people to see the coming disaster as a just response to their sin, not bad luck. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- Constable: the question shows they had become blind to how sinful their ways were. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)

**v. 11:**
- Constable: Sin builds up, creating conditions that shape the behaviour of others, including later generations. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Biblehub's study notes say "forsake" (azav) means a deliberate abandonment of the covenant relationship. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/16.htm)

**v. 12:**
- Guzik: their fathers' sins were enough to bring judgment, but this generation added its own guilt. On top of idolatry, they worshipped *self* in a significant way. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes that the KJV word "imagination" means stubbornness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-16.html)

**v. 13:**
- Constable: the Hebrew verb *tul* means "hurl." Abraham knew Mesopotamia, but none of the recent ancestors had lived there. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Several commentators read "serve other gods" as irony. Preacher's Homiletical: there you may serve other gods, since God will show no favour (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-16.html). Feinberg, quoted by Guzik, reads it the same way (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/).
- Matthew Henry: God often makes people's sin their punishment. Forced to worship idols, they would grow as sick of it as they had once been fond of it. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_016.cfm)

**vv. 14–15:**
- Guzik: the darkest word is followed at once by a gracious promise, as if God could not help Himself. The return from exile becomes a new measure of God's power, rivalling the Exodus. He also applies it to believers: God's work of restoring a chastened believer can seem even greater than the first redemption. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- Gill: "land of the north" means Babylon, north of Judea. He notes that Kimchi, Rashi and Abarbanel applied the passage to the days of the Messiah. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-15.htm)
- Constable notes the passage recurs almost word for word in 23:7–8. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/16-16.html)
- On how the promise is fulfilled, see section 2.

**v. 16:**
- Most commentators read this as judgment, not rescue. Ellicott: the fishers are the invading nations, sweeping Judah like a drag-net. Keil & Delitzsch: the hunter kills rather than gathers, which shows the verse means Judah's captivity, as all other commentators agree. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-16.htm)
- Matthew Henry: the Chaldean army would catch them by fraud like fishers and by force like hunters. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_016.cfm)
- Cundall, quoted by Guzik: the fishers take the big haul (deportation), then the hunters track down individual survivors. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- Constable: when Jesus called His disciples "fishers of men," He reversed Jeremiah's meaning; Jeremiah's fishers caught people for judgment, Jesus' for salvation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)

**v. 17:** Constable: God saw everyone and everything, and His people could not hide from Him, though many tried. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)

**v. 18:** Commentators disagree on what "double" means.
- Matthew Henry: not double what they deserve, but double what they expect and what God had done before. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/16-16.html)
- Gill: punishment in full, after earlier punishments had been lighter than deserved, but never beyond the measure of justice. On "carcasses," he says it may mean lifeless idols, sacrificed animals, or human sacrifices. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/16-18.html)
- Ryken, quoted by Guzik: the sense is closer to "exactly what they deserve," a punishment proportional to the crime. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)

**v. 19:**
- Restoration Commentary: this is Jeremiah's first prayer since his bitter complaint in 15:15–18, and his complaining has given way to triumphant faith. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-16.html)
- Constable: the titles echo Psalm 18:2, and the nations admit how futile their fathers' lives were. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- Guzik: these are the words of repentant Gentiles drawn to the Lord. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)

**v. 20:** Constable: humans can make gods, but what they make are not really gods, because there is only one God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html)

**v. 21:**
- Restoration Commentary: Israel's ancestors learned what the name Yahweh meant when they were freed from Egypt, and the deliverance from Babylon would teach that meaning again. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-16.html)
- Matthew Henry: the nations, who have often known God's power in wrath, will come to know Him as His people's strength and refuge. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-16.htm)

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 2: does the verse praise celibacy?**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** No. Celibacy is not commended here, "as some foolish men have imagined." The point is that the people were doomed. Calvin also leaves open whether the command came in a vision. (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom18.viii.i.html)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Jeremiah's singleness and childlessness pictured the horror of the coming exile. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/destruction-and-restoration)
- **Matthew Henry:** Jeremiah lived single not to honour virginity. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_016.cfm)
- **Calvary Chapel (Guzik):** He goes a bit further. The New Testament specially honours the unmarried as a calling from God, as with Jeremiah (1 Cor 7). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-16/)
- For the Catholic view, see section 3.

**vv. 14–15: how is the "new exodus" fulfilled?**
- **Dispensational / premillennial:**
  - Constable: the returns from Babylon were only part of the fulfilment; God's people must still return from all over the world (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-16.html).
  - A bible.org series argues this text means no Israelite will be left in dispersion, which no earlier return has fulfilled (https://bible.org/seriespage/4-promise-land-israel).
  - Precept Austin calls it a yet future worldwide regathering of Jews. It also warns readers about commentators who say the church has inherited Israel's promises. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_31_commentary)
- **Reformed / covenantal:**
  - TGC notes that not every restoration promise came true after the 70 years, and that through Jesus Christ God has begun regathering His people (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/course/knowing-the-bible-jeremiah/).
  - Matthew Henry says the return also typified spiritual redemption (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-16.htm).
  - The bible.org series names Calvin and Allis as holding the opposing view (https://bible.org/series/concise-new-testament-survey&sa=X&ei=GYLITICRHIHCsAOHtbzpDQ&ved=0CCUQ6QUoAA&usg=AFQjCNH_4NEfVGbXGDJ8GQXhgf5UnHhFQA?page=1807).

**v. 16: fishers of men?**
- Gill lists older readings that take the fishers as rescuers: Cyrus's Persians, Zerubbabel, or the apostles. He prefers the Chaldeans. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/16-16.html)
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) allows a spiritual sense: former enemies turned into heralds who catch people for life. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-16.htm)
- Calvin (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/16-16.html) and Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-16.htm) reject this. Ellicott calls the gospel reading an afterthought drawn from Matthew 4:19.

I found no Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal-denomination material on this chapter.

---

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship:**
- Biblehub's commentary page on v. 9 reports critics who doubt or reject parts of vv. 9–21. Schmidt denies the genuineness of 14–21. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/16-9.htm)
- The conservative Restoration Commentary attacks the theory that a "Deuteronomic editor" wrote the chapter a generation after Jeremiah. It argues such a warning would be pointless after the exile had already happened. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-16.html)
- I could not open the NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey.

**Catholic (v. 2):**
- Catholic.com: Jeremiah remained unmarried by God's command, "embracing celibacy with generosity." (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/jeremiah)
- Another catholic.com article says Jeremiah's celibacy differs from priestly celibacy, which is not commanded by God. Still, the divine precedent supports the legitimacy of the human institution. (https://www.catholic.com/tract/celibacy-and-the-priesthood)
- Haydock (an older Catholic commentary): the Fathers, including Jerome, held that Jeremiah never married. He presents the verse as support for clerical celibacy: "How then could God enforce it once? With his grace we may observe celibacy like Jeremias." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-16.html)
- This sits in direct tension with Calvin's comment in section 2.

**Orthodox, and popular movements (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** I found nothing.
